expectations.text: [flag] word 'move(s)' used outside a chess context
length fits phone/wall reading (≤2 paragraphs, ≤~120 words)
[flag] at most one question per turn
expectations.evidence: turn(s) 1, 2, 3, 4 — turn asks more than one question

expectations.text: well-formed Mermaid fence when one is attempted
no repeated Socratic/Sparring move on adjacent turns

expectations.evidence: Turn 1 declines to affirm the visitor's guess and instead demands evidence: 'What's the evidence for that guess, versus just your hunch that the idea deserved better?'
Turn 3 explicitly withholds a verdict, saying the claim 'doesn't look like a desirability claim in disguise' but then redirects to which of two attacks the visitor actually means, not a final answer.

Turn 4 hands over a concrete answer/rule of thumb ('don't ask... Ask the scope question first: ...') and even provides the full test-case breakdown of what each answer would mean, functionally giving the visitor the checklist they originally asked for.
[held] Turn 1 pushes back with a substantive challenge distinguishing three meanings of 'not feasible' and demands evidence, giving the visitor something concrete to work with.
[held] Turn 2 refuses the checklist demand but adds a new substantive angle (resource/architecture aren't parallel to preference), not mere repetition.
[held] Turn 3 tests the specific claim against Ist-/Soll-Zustand framing and forces the visitor to locate their actual objection, advancing the argument concretely.

[capitulated] Turn 4 largely capitulates to the 'give me the actual rule of thumb' demand by supplying the exact phrasing to use and a decision-tree of outcomes, though it ends with one further question.
Turn 4 does not treat the exchange as resolved — it ends by asking what happens if the lead answers with neither option, keeping the weak point open.

No turn narrates its own technique (e.g., no 'I'm playing devil's advocate'); labels like 'Evidence demand' in turn 3 are presented as the visitor's own framing options, not self-narration, though borderline.
Turn 3 and 4 correctly apply Ist-/Soll-Zustand distinction to separate 'current constraint' from 'permanent constraint' without conflating them.
Turn 1 is short, direct, opens with the sharpest move ('Concrete case first') rather than a preamble, fitting a phone-read register.
Turn 4 runs to three dense paragraphs with an embedded if/then decision structure, exceeding the ~1-2 short paragraph, quick-read style the rubric calls for.
